The Bible: Textual Transmission and Historical Evidence

The "Bible" is not one book. The transmission question must be answered separately for the Hebrew Bible / Old Testament and the Greek New Testament, because their evidence is very different.

Part A — The Hebrew Bible / Old Testament

The evidence base

  • Masoretic Text (MT): the standardized Hebrew tradition fixed by the Masoretes (c. 7th–10th c. CE). Key codices: Aleppo Codex (c. 920 CE), Leningrad Codex (1008 CE — the basis of printed Hebrew Bibles).
  • Dead Sea Scrolls (DSS): c. 250 BCE – 68 CE, found at Qumran. They push physical evidence back roughly a thousand years earlier than the great Masoretic codices.
  • Septuagint (LXX): Greek translation of the Hebrew, begun c. 3rd c. BCE.
  • Samaritan Pentateuch (SP): an independent Torah tradition.

What the evidence shows

  • Strong stability where it can be tested. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) is ~1,000 years older than the medieval MT yet is substantially the same text; differences are overwhelmingly spelling, word order, and minor wording.
  • But genuine textual pluriformity existed before standardization. At Qumran the OT circulated in multiple text-types. The LXX of Jeremiah is ~1/7 shorter and arranged differently than the MT; 1–2 Samuel shows substantial LXX/Qumran variation; Psalm numbering and some passages differ. The "one stable Hebrew text" only becomes the dominant reality after roughly the 1st–2nd c. CE.
  • Composition vs. transmission. Mainstream critical scholarship holds that the Pentateuch and many OT books are composite, edited from multiple sources/traditions over centuries (the broad legacy of the Documentary Hypothesis and its successors). This is a compositional issue, distinct from copying fidelity.

Net for the OT: transmission from the standardization era onward is demonstrably conservative; before standardization the text was plural, and the deeper academic debate is about composition and editing, not about medieval scribes corrupting a once-pristine text.

Part B — The Greek New Testament

The evidence base (unmatched in antiquity)

  • ~5,800+ Greek manuscripts, plus ~10,000+ Latin and thousands in other versions, plus tens of thousands of patristic quotations.
  • Earliest fragments very early: P52 (John, c. 125–175 CE); major papyri (P45, P46, P66, P75) from the late 2nd–3rd c.; great codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus 4th c.
  • No other work of antiquity is even close in manuscript volume or in the gap between composition and earliest copies.

The variant problem — stated honestly

  • There are an estimated ~400,000 textual variants — more variants than words in the NT. This is the apologetic Muslim camp's strongest factual point and must not be minimized.
  • However, the overwhelming majority are: spelling, word order (Greek is inflected, so order rarely changes meaning), nonsense scribal slips, and synonyms. The number is large mainly because the manuscript pool is huge.
  • Variants that are both meaningful and viable are a small fraction. The few theologically weighty ones are well known and openly printed in modern Bibles' footnotes:
  • Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7–8) — an explicit Trinity proof-text; not original, a late Latin insertion. Modern scholarship and modern Bibles reject it.
  • Longer ending of Mark (16:9–20) and the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) — almost certainly not original to those Gospels; flagged in every critical edition.
  • Luke 22:43–44, 1 Tim 3:16, John 1:18 — text-critically contested.

The scholarly dispute

  • Bart Ehrman (Misquoting Jesus; The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture) argues some variants are theologically motivated ("orthodox corruptions") and that certainty about the exact original wording is limited.
  • Daniel Wallace, Bruce Metzger, Larry Hurtado counter that the sheer manuscript abundance lets scholars reconstruct the early text with high confidence, and that — as Ehrman himself concedes in interviews — no cardinal Christian doctrine stands or falls on a textually disputed passage (the doctrines are taught in many undisputed passages).
  • Both camps agree on the data; they disagree on how much interpretive significance to assign it.

Arbiter verdict — Bible transmission

Present.

  • Defense: unparalleled manuscript evidence, early attestation, a reconstructable early text, and full scholarly transparency about the disputed passages.
  • Prosecution: hundreds of thousands of variants, a few doctrinally sensitive ones, no autographs, and a composite/edited OT.

Weigh.

  • The claim "the NT message was textually fabricated or wholesale altered" is not supported by the manuscript evidence — it proves the opposite (we can trace and isolate changes precisely because we have so many copies).
  • The claim "the transmitted text is not letter-perfect and a few theologically loaded passages are demonstrably later" is well supported and conceded by mainstream scholarship.
  • The OT's real academic vulnerability is composition and pre-1st-century pluriformity, not medieval copying.

Judge. On the narrow historical question — can the early text be recovered, and was the core message transmitted intact? — the evidence favors the reliability side: the NT is the best-attested ancient text and its substantive content is recoverable and stable. On the purity claim — the text we hold is identical to the autographs in every word — the evidence favors the critics: it demonstrably is not, and Christianity's own scholars say so in print. The honest position is therefore split by question, and any argument that uses NT variants to imply invention of the message proves too much and fails (Methodology §4).
